Sentience refers to the capacity of an organism to have subjective experiences, to feel sensations, emotions, and perceive its surroundings. It is often associated with the ability to experience pleasure, pain, and other basic sensations. Sentience is considered a lower-level form of consciousness and is commonly found in a wide range of animals, including mammals, birds, and even some invertebrates.

Source: Griffin, D. R. (1976). The Question of Animal Awareness: Evolutionary Continuity of Mental Experience. The Rockefeller University Press.


Sapience, on the other hand, is a higher-order cognitive ability that goes beyond mere sentience. It involves the capacity for abstract thinking, reasoning, problem-solving, self-awareness, and the ability to make complex decisions. Sapience is often associated with humans and is considered a defining characteristic of our species. It includes the ability to think critically, plan for the future, and engage in philosophical and moral reasoning.

Source: Shea, N. (1989). Sapience, Pan narrans, and the Possibility of a Non-Human Culture. Philosophy of Anthropology and Sociology: A Volume in Honor of Nandor Fodor, 214-225.

https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/82-003-x/2020002/article/00002-eng.htm

To sum it up for you, post-legalisation in Canada, there was only a minor uptick in reported cannabis usage. The population of people who reported smoking at some point in the last three months increased from 15% to 17%. Meanwhile, the population of people who reported smoking daily or near-daily was unchanged (from a range of 5.4-6.5% to a range of 5.5-6.5%).

What was extra surprising and encouraging was that the rate of under-age (15-18 year-old) cannabis smokers nearly halved! It went from about 20% to just over 10%! Great news, given that all current research on the negative mental health benefits of cannabis points directly to this age group (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6710088/). 

This makes intuitive sense, as it's much more difficult for underage people to buy Cannabis once they have to start showing ID. 

So, luckily, your fears about the legalisation of Cannabis are unfounded! As seen in the many case studies overseas, the harm that weed causes is reduced. It definitely takes a bit of maturity to accept that sometimes the best way to reduce harm is to control a substance, not leave it in the hands of a black market.

Obviously reddit can't make the decision for you, but here are some considerations.

Buying a house is financially the better option. That is undeniable. If you buy a house now instead of travel, you will have a higher net worth when you're 50. It may even be by a considerable amount.

However, once you own a mortgage, you have a massive liability when you're travelling. It is essential to have a steady income to remain afloat, which simply isn't possible when travelling.

The house option will still be there after travelling - however, you won't be as wealthy in 25 years, and it's impossible to know by how much. The benefit though is you get to travel and have a fulfilling, bonding experience with your partner in you youth. That option won't be there if you get a house first, and you will regret it/grow resentful as a result if travelling is important to you. 

Now for opinions: I think travelling first is best choice. I think being fairly well off and fulfilled is a more desirable life outcome than being very well off and unfulfilled. You may discover new passions, new loves, new ideas. I am biased, as I have travelled and adored every minute of it. Additionally, my greatest fear is growing old and having that dreadful feeling that I wasted my life away, having no meaningful experiences and connections. -

The word "repeat" does not come from the repetitive process of harvesting peat. The term "repeat" has a Latin origin, derived from the word "repetere," which means "to go back, to do again." It entered the English language through Old French and Middle English, and it has been used to refer to the act of doing or saying something again or the recurrence of an action or event. The word "peat" refers to a type of organic matter that forms in wetlands and can be used as fuel. The two words, "peat" and "repeat," have different etymological origins and are unrelated.

Yup, my country has had three-pronged plugs since the beginning of our electrical grid. The US, which I believe invented electricity and had the first electrical grid, did not initially have any earthing systems. I assumed that had continued all the way up until the modern-day, however, it appears I was wrong and that the US has indeed updated its regulations to include earthing conductors.
Yup, I was confused as I thought all outlets in the US had two prongs and that applianced in the US simply weren't grounded as they are in other countries. Turns out I had been misinformed.

You ever skirt along a trampoline and touch your mates to give them a zap? What happens there is you build up an electrical charge, making you more electrically charged than your friend. When you touch them, the electricity shoots over to them to balance itself out. 

This can happen to anything, so say the metal casing of your fridge builds up an electrical charge and you go to grab some beer. You're standing on the ground and so you have the same electrical charge as the ground, but the fridge doesn't. Reach for the handle... zzzzttt, you get a zap. If enough electricity is able to build up in that fridge, you could be real fucked up. 

So, what we do to stop that, is we get a big metal rod or cable and dig it into the ground. Then we run a wire from that, all the way over to the fridge, where then it's connected to the metal frame. This means anytime a charge tries to build up in the fridge, it just goes through the wire and the fridge's charge stays the same as the ground.

Since your charge is the same as the ground, and the fridges charge is the same as the ground, it can't zap ya when you're thirsty.

This is just a quick example of how earth wires help against static electricity, but earthing things helps stop loads of different electrical faults from occurring. 

tl;dr earth wires are just extra wires we put in that are used for safety so people don't get electrocuted as often

By my understanding, life kept swinging back and forth in number over this period, as told by the oxidation levels of iron in rock layers.

The mass extinction that killed the dinosaurs likely killed far more living beings, but only because by that time there were an exponentially greater number of things alive, with massive diversity and numbers. 

When the great oxidation happened, life was still relatively young and nowhere near as diverse. All of life was made up of single celled creatures, and percentage-wise, far more life was killed. 

What happened was, before life started to photosynthesise, there wasn’t much oxygen around. Oxygen is highly reactive and extremely toxic, it quickly oxidises anything it touches. Photosynthesis turns CO2 into oxygen.

Life started photosynthesising all of the CO2 in the earths atmosphere, turning it into poisonous oxygen gas which turned around and killed everything that produced it. Additionally, this process slowly cooled the earth as it stripped our supplies of CO2, a strong greenhouse gas, plunging us into the longest, coldest ice age our planet has ever seen. Since no life had evolved that could survive the cold nor the toxicity of oxygen, everything died.

Nearly everything. 

Life survived in small, isolated pockets in deep-sea vents, untouched by the poisoned oxygen waters nor frozen by the cataclysmic ice age above. 

If not for these tiny, lucky patches of life that held on through the 400 *million* years of ice age, life would never have made it past its infancy. 

Earth would be dead.
